bug(sdk-python): update_current_span overwrites third-party observation type — openinference AGENT/TOOL spans ingested as SPAN
body:
### Describe the bug

`update_current_span()` (and the other `update_current_*` helpers) permanently downgrade the observation type of spans created by third-party OTel instrumentation.

When the current OTel span was created by an external instrumentor — e.g. `openinference-instrumentation-agno`, which marks spans with `openinference.span.kind = AGENT | TOOL | CHAIN | RETRIEVER | LLM | ...` — it has no `langfuse.observation.type` attribute. `Langfuse._get_observation_type_from_otel_span()` only looks at `langfuse.observation.type` and falls back to `"span"`, so `_get_span_class()` returns `LangfuseSpan`, and `LangfuseObservationWrapper.__init__` then *writes* `langfuse.observation.type = "span"` onto the span.

The write is the problem: `openinference.span.kind = AGENT` is still on the span, but the explicit Langfuse attribute now wins, so the observation is ingested as SPAN instead of AGENT.

This is silent and order-dependent: in our app, agent spans (`<Agent>.arun`) are typed SPAN because our pre-hooks call `update_current_span(metadata=…)` on them, while tool spans — which no hook touches — keep their correct TOOL type. So the same trace shows a mix of correctly and incorrectly typed observations, which makes it look like an instrumentation bug rather than an SDK one.

**Expected behavior:** `update_current_span(...)` should update attributes without changing the observation type. Concretely, when the span carries no `langfuse.observation.type`:

- either fall back to `openinference.span.kind` when resolving the observation type (`AGENT → agent`, `TOOL → tool`, `CHAIN → chain`, `RETRIEVER → retriever`, `LLM → generation`, `EMBEDDING → embedding`, `GUARDRAIL → guardrail`, `EVALUATOR → evaluator`) — all of these already exist in `ObservationTypeLiteral`;
- or don't write `langfuse.observation.type` at all when the caller didn't ask for a type change, leaving the ingestion-side mapping of `openinference.span.kind` intact.

### Steps to reproduce

Minimal repro, no

title: V4 historic backfill fails with non-default ClickHouse databases
body:
When Langfuse runs in clustered ClickHouse mode with CLICKHOUSE_DB set to a
non-default database, such as `langfuse`, the V4 historic backfill creates the
scratch table in the correct database but later executes unqualified
SYSTEM STOP MERGES and SYSTEM SYNC REPLICA commands.

Distributed DDL workers resolve those commands against the `default` database,
causing:

Table default.observations_pid_tid_sorting does not exist

All V4 backfill DDL and scratch-table references should explicitly qualify the
configured ClickHouse database.

title: Worker: Redis reconnect storm — connections retry without jitter, ~4,800 log lines from a 15s outage
body:
### Describe the bug

When the Redis host becomes temporarily unresolvable, `langfuse-worker` emits a
very large burst of identical connection errors in a few seconds. The per-connection
backoff appears to work correctly; what seems to be missing is **jitter**, so all
of the worker's Redis connections retry in lockstep.

I hit this on a self-hosted Docker Compose deployment where Redis is a sibling
container. A routine image bump recreates the Redis container, its DNS name
disappears for ~15 seconds, and the worker produces roughly 4,800 log lines in
that window.

### Measurements

From a single incident (Redis unavailable 16:30:43 → 16:30:58, ~15s):

- ~4,800 lines total, **2,430 within one minute**
- **20 errors inside a 35ms span**:

```
16:30:50.253  16:30:50.253  16:30:50.254  16:30:50.257  16:30:50.260
16:30:50.262  16:30:50.263  16:30:50.268  16:30:50.269  16:30:50.270
```

Each failure logs two lines:

```
Error: getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND langfuse-redis
<timestamp> error   Redis error getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND langfuse-redis
```

Individual connections do space their retries (~1.2s apart, consistent with
ioredis' default `retryStrategy`). The volume comes from many connections — the
worker appears to hold roughly one per BullMQ queue — all failing at the same
instant and therefore all retrying at the same instant.

### Expected behaviour

A brief Redis outage should produce a bounded amount of log output. Adding
jitter to the ioredis `retryStrategy` would spread reconnects out, and
optionally collapsing repeated identical connection errors would help further.

### Why this is awkward to work around

Self-hosting exposes `REDIS_COMMAND_TIMEOUT`, `REDIS_REQUEST_SOCKET_TIMEOUT_MS`
and `REDIS_BLOCKING_SOCKET_TIMEOUT_MS`, but nothing for retry or backoff policy,
so `retryStrategy` cannot be adjusted from outside the image. I have worked
around it by rate-limiting these lines in my log shipper, which is not ideal
since it also caps genuine outages.

Happy to test a patch

title: feat: price server-side web-search tool calls (Anthropic web_search_requests, OpenAI web_search)
body:
### Feature request

Add a price key for **server-side web-search tool calls** to the Langfuse-managed Anthropic model definitions (and ideally the OpenAI ones), the same way the managed Gemini definitions already price grounding.

### Why

Server-side web search is billed as a **per-request fee that no token count can express**. Langfuse already models exactly this for Google — `gemini-3.1-pro-preview` carries `grounding_queries` / `web_search_queries` / `webSearchQueries` at `$0.014`, so a grounded Gemini generation prices correctly end to end.

Anthropic has the identical billing shape and no equivalent key. `claude-sonnet-4-6`'s managed definition currently exposes only token keys:

```
input, input_tokens, output, output_tokens,
cache_creation_input_tokens, input_cache_creation, input_cache_creation_5m, input_cache_creation_1h,
cache_read_input_tokens, input_cached_tokens, input_cache_read
```

Anthropic prices its `web_search` server tool at **$10 / 1,000 searches** ($0.01 each), published on the pricing page alongside the token rates. That fee is currently unrepresentable in Langfuse, so every grounded Claude generation is silently under-priced by the entire search component.

This is not a rounding error. On grounded search workloads the fee is routinely a large fraction of a call's true cost — on one of our Gemini observations, 23 search queries at the managed $0.014 came to **76% of that observation's total cost**. The Anthropic equivalent is invisible today.

### Proposed keys

Following the existing convention of mirroring the provider's own field name:

| Anthropic | `web_search_requests` | `usage.server_tool_use.web_search_requests` on the Messages API response | $0.01 |

title: Trace-level input/output/name overwritten by last-ingested LangChain root when multiple processes share one trace id (distributed multi-agent)
body:
### Describe the bug

In a distributed multi-agent setup, several independent processes contribute observations to the same trace id. Each process runs its own `langfuse.langchain.CallbackHandler` against a LangGraph app, and downstream processes join the caller's trace using `trace_context={"trace_id", "parent_span_id"}`.
 
The observation tree is correct: one root span, and each downstream agent's spans are correctly parented under the caller's span with the shared trace id. But the trace-level `input`, `output`, and `name` shown on the Trace record are taken from whichever process's LangChain root chain is ingested last, not from the process that actually owns the root of the trace.
 
I confirmed on the raw OTLP spans that only the originating (root) process emits trace-level attributes:
 
- Root process span has `langfuse.trace.input`, `langfuse.trace.output`, and `langfuse.trace.name` set to the originating request/response.
- Downstream (delegated) process spans do **not** emit `langfuse.trace.input`/`output`.
 
Despite that, the resulting Trace record's `input`/`output` are the downstream specialist's request/response, and without a propagated trace name the trace `name` also becomes the downstream chain's name.
 
Each process-local LangGraph root observation carries `metadata.is_langchain_root = true`. It appears the backend derives trace-level `input`/`output`/`name` from a LangChain-root observation regardless of whether that observation is the true root of the trace id (i.e., regardless of `parent_span_id` linking it beneath another process's span). The last such observation to be ingested wins, which in a fan-out is a non-deterministic specialist.
 

### Steps to reproduce

1. Stand up two services, A (orchestrator) and B (specialist), each with its own process, OTel `TracerProvider`, and `langfuse.langchain.CallbackHandler`. Export via OTLP to a collector that forwards to Langfuse with `x-langfuse-ingestion-version: 4`.
2. In A, start a root observation

### Describe the bug

When saving a default evaluation model, Langfuse reports that the model configuration is valid even when the model produced no structured output.

This occurs when an OpenAI-compatible provider returns `finish_reason: "length"` with an empty `message.content`. The configuration test succeeds, but real evaluator executions later fail with `AI_NoOutputGeneratedError`.

The model configuration test should read and validate the generated structured output. If no output was generated, saving should fail with the same error that the evaluator worker would raise.

The model is saved successfully even though the response contains no final output.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Run self-hosted Langfuse v4.1.0.

title: bug: `createChatPrompt` MCP tool does not support `placeholder` messages like the SDK
body:
### Describe the bug

**Description**

The `createChatPrompt` MCP tool (langfuse-mcp server) cannot create "placeholder" messages in chat prompts.
Its input schema for `prompt` items only allows `{role: string, content: string}` (both required, `additionalProperties: false`), but Langfuse chat prompts support a distinct placeholder message shape `{type: "placeholder", name: "<variable>"}` that we use to inject images. Since the tool schema has no way to express this shape, any MCP client is unable to add, edit, or preserve placeholder messages in chat prompts.

As a consequence, if a chat prompt containing a placeholder is first created via the Langfuse UI, and an agent later creates a new version of that same prompt through the `createChatPrompt` MCP tool, the placeholder message is kept from the new version but is broken forever. The only workaround we found is to delete the prompt entirely and recreate it from scratch.

**Expected behavior**

The `createChatPrompt` MCP tool schema should support the placeholder message shape `{type: "placeholder", name: string}` alongside `{role, content}`, so that:
- Placeholder messages can be created/edited through MCP, matching what's possible in the UI.
- Creating a new version of a prompt that already contains a placeholder preserves that placeholder instead of dropping it.

**Primary repro**

1. Connect an MCP client (e.g. Claude Code) to the `langfuse-mcp` server (Langfuse Cloud, `https://cloud.langfuse.com/api/public/mcp`).

title: docs: experiments data model does not mention that only one run item per dataset item is readable in a run
body:
### Which package is this about?

Docs — [Experiments Data Model](https://langfuse.com/docs/evaluation/experiments/data-model)

### Describe the problem

The Experiments data model page models the run/run-item relation as one-to-many:

```
DatasetRun "1" --> "n" DatasetRunItem
```

and the `DatasetRunItem` table documents a uniqueness constraint only on `id`. Nothing on the page says that **at most one run item per `datasetItemId` is readable within a run**, even though several can be written.

That gap is easy to fall into, because the write path gives no signal at all:

1. `POST /api/public/dataset-run-items` with `runName=X`, `datasetItemId=Y`, `traceId=A` → 200, returns run item id `5f98191b…`
2. Same `runName` + `datasetItemId`, `traceId=B` → 200, returns a **different** id `432f3957…`
3. `GET` the run → `totalItems: 1`, and which row comes back varies between reads.

Both writes succeed and are stored; the read collapses them (the `LIMIT 1 BY …` noted in #9319). A user sampling each case N times sees N traces and N sets of scores land correctly, then finds one row per case in the dataset-run table — and reasonably concludes their repetitions never ran, rather than that the platform does not model them.

This was confirmed as intended behaviour in #9319 ("not a bug but a limitation by design. Our application code currently does not support repetitions"), with the feature request tracked in #5855. That answer lives in a closed issue, though — not in the docs anyone reads first.

### Suggested fix

On the Experiments data model page (and ideally in the `dataset-run-items` API reference), state that a dataset run surfaces at most one run item per dataset item, that additional run items for the same item are accepted but not returned, and link #5855 for repetitions support. A one-line note under the `DatasetRunItem` table would have saved us a fair amount of debugging.

### Additional information

Reproduced against Langfuse Cloud on 2026-08-10. Related: #5855, #12

Root cause (traced through source on main): web/src/features/evals/hooks/useEvalConfigFilterOptions.ts fetches dropdown options via api.traces.filterOptions that procedure (web/src/server/api/routers/traces.ts) calls getTracesGroupedByName whose query (packages/shared/src/server/repositories/traces.ts) is select name, count(*) from traces t … — the legacy traces table, which is empty on events-only instances an events-table variant already exists — getEventsGroupedByTraceName in packages/shared/src/server/repositories/events.ts — but traces.filterOptions never routes to it (its input schema has no useEventsTable flag, unlike other procedures in the same router) Expected: trace-name options aggregated from the events table on events-only instances (the matching side already works — the worker compares against the observation's trace_name, so a manually-constructed filter matches fine). title: [bug] Sandbox provider lifecycle hooks are never invoked, leaking runtime sessions
body:
## Summary
The sandbox provider lifecycle hooks are defined but never invoked. `createInAppAgentSandbox` returns `onTurnEnded`, but that callback only persists `providerSessionId`; it never calls the provider's `suspendSession` hook. No production caller for `suspendSession` or `terminateSession` was found.

## Code reference
- `packages/shared/src/in-app-agent/server/sandbox/service.ts:69-77` — `onTurnEnded` only calls `persistState()`.
- `packages/shared/src/in-app-agent/server/sandbox/types.ts:58-66` — documents `suspendSession` as releasing live runtime resources and `terminateSession` as permanent teardown.
- `packages/shared/src/in-app-agent/server/sandbox/providers/docker.ts:211-228` and `lambdaMicrovm.ts:284-332` — implement those hooks.

## Reproduction
1. Enable a sandbox provider and execute a sandbox tool in a conversation.
2. End the agent turn.
3. Inspect the provider: Docker containers remain running, and the Lambda provider is never asked to suspend the microVM.

## Expected behavior
After a turn, the provider lifecycle should suspend the session while retaining its persisted identifier for reuse; permanent cleanup should call `terminateSession` when the conversation/session is deleted.

## Actual behavior
Only the database state is persisted. The provider hooks are unreachable from production code, so live runtime resources are not released.

## Why it matters
A Docker container can remain running per conversation until manually removed, causing resource exhaustion. The Lambda provider's in-memory session map and remote microVM lifecycle also never receive the intended cleanup signal. The provider contract and the in-app-agent README therefore describe behavior that does not occur.

## Suggested fix
Wire `onTurnEnded` to an idempotent `suspendSession` call and add the corresponding termination path, with error handling and tests asserting both provider hooks are invoked.

title: [bug] Sandbox runtime races on the global tool_calls directory
body:
## Summary
The sandbox runtime uses one global `/workspace/tool_calls` directory for every HTTP request, while the HTTP server handles requests concurrently. Each request deletes and recreates that directory before executing its operation, so overlapping sandbox calls can observe or destroy another request's files.

## Code reference
- `packages/in-app-agent-sandbox-runtime/src/server.ts:28-62` — asynchronous HTTP handler with no request/session serialization.
- `packages/in-app-agent-sandbox-runtime/src/server.ts:71-85` — `syncToolCallFiles` recursively removes and recreates the global directory.
- `packages/in-app-agent-sandbox-runtime/src/server.ts:135-145` — every `/sandbox` request synchronizes that shared directory before running.
- `packages/shared/src/in-app-agent/server/sandbox/providers/lambdaMicrovm.ts:199-213` — sends tool-call files on every operation.

## Reproduction
Send two `/sandbox` POST requests concurrently with different `toolCallFiles` payloads. For example, have request A run `cat tool_calls/a.txt` after supplying `a.txt`, and request B supply `b.txt` at the same time.

## Expected behavior
Each operation should see an atomic snapshot of the files belonging to its own session/request.

## Actual behavior
The requests race on `rm(TOOL_CALLS_ROOT)` and file writes. The last synchronization wins; an in-flight command can see the other request's files or get missing-file errors.

## Why it matters
Concurrent model tool calls can produce incorrect results, corrupt per-turn context, or expose one operation's input to another. The runtime package has no concurrency tests.

## Suggested fix
Serialize operations per runtime/session or use request/session-scoped directories with an atomic handoff. Add a concurrent-request regression test with distinct file snapshots.

title: [bug] Sandbox command timeout leaves descendant processes running
body:
## Summary
The sandbox runtime's command timeout kills only the shell process, not its descendant process tree.

## Code reference
- `packages/in-app-agent-sandbox-runtime/src/server.ts:297-310` — starts `sh -lc` without a process group/session.
- `packages/in-app-agent-sandbox-runtime/src/server.ts:344-361` — timeout calls `child.kill(SIGKILL)` and returns exit code 124.

## Reproduction
Run a bash operation with a short timeout, such as `sleep 300 & wait`, using `timeoutMs: 50`. After the operation returns exit code 124, inspect processes inside the sandbox.

## Expected behavior
A timed-out command should terminate the complete process tree and leave no child process running after the tool reports failure.

## Actual behavior
Only the shell is killed. Background descendants can survive and continue consuming resources or mutating the workspace after the tool has returned a timeout.

## Why it matters
The runtime is long-lived, so repeated timed-out commands can exhaust CPU/memory and cause post-timeout writes that the agent believes did not happen.

## Suggested fix
Start commands in a process group and kill the group/tree on timeout. Add a regression test covering a background child.

title: [bug] Lambda MicroVM sandbox requests have no timeout
body:
## Summary
The Lambda MicroVM sandbox provider has no timeout or abort signal on either operation requests or bridge health probes. The bridge loop has a nominal deadline, but one hung `fetch` can block beyond it.

## Code reference
- `packages/shared/src/in-app-agent/server/sandbox/providers/lambdaMicrovm.ts:199-213` — operation `fetch` has no `AbortSignal` or timeout.
- `packages/shared/src/in-app-agent/server/sandbox/providers/lambdaMicrovm.ts:336-394` — `waitForBridge` checks `BRIDGE_READY_TIMEOUT_MS`, but its health `fetch` at lines 366-374 is unbounded.

## Reproduction
Point a Lambda MicroVM endpoint or proxy at a server that accepts the connection but never sends a response. Start a sandbox operation, or create a session while the bridge health endpoint hangs.

## Expected behavior
Each outbound request should fail within a bounded time, and the bridge readiness deadline should remain effective.

## Actual behavior
The awaited `fetch` can remain pending indefinitely, blocking the worker's agent execution and preventing the readiness loop from reaching its deadline.

## Why it matters
A stalled proxy or microVM can hold a worker job and its resources indefinitely, reducing agent throughput and making recovery dependent on process restart.

## Suggested fix
Use an abortable per-request timeout, ensure the bridge deadline covers the request itself, and add tests for a hung operation and hung health probe.

title: [bug] Admin access webhook failures suppress retries and can hang requests
body:
## Summary
Admin access webhook delivery is awaited on request paths without a timeout, and failed deliveries are marked as recently sent before the request succeeds. A failed webhook therefore suppresses retries for 24 hours.

## Code reference
- `web/src/server/adminAccessWebhook.ts:19-29` — records the dedupe timestamp before delivery.
- `web/src/server/adminAccessWebhook.ts:54-81` — awaits `fetch` without an abort timeout and only logs failures.
- Callers await this helper in `web/src/server/api/trpc.ts:329,357,453,620,706`, `web/src/pages/api/dashboard/execute-query-stream.ts:91,101`, and `web/src/features/traces/server/buildTraceExport.ts:156`.
- Existing tests cover success, duplicate, and non-OK responses but not retry-after-failure or a hung endpoint.

## Reproduction
1. Configure `LANGFUSE_ADMIN_ACCESS_WEBHOOK` to an endpoint that returns HTTP 500 or never responds.
2. Trigger an admin access event.
3. Trigger the same event again within 24 hours.

## Expected behavior
A failed delivery should be retryable, and an unresponsive webhook should not block the user-facing request indefinitely.

## Actual behavior
The first attempt stores the dedupe key before `fetch`; failures do not clear it. The second attempt is skipped for 24 hours. A hanging fetch remains awaited with no application-level deadline.

## Why it matters
Security/admin notifications can be silently lost, while project access, dashboard, and export operations can stall behind an external endpoint.

## Suggested fix
Only commit the dedupe timestamp after a successful delivery (or clear it on failure), add a bounded abort timeout, and test both failure retry and hung-endpoint behavior.

title: [bug] Mixpanel flush can hang indefinitely on an unresponsive endpoint
body:
## Summary
`MixpanelClient.sendBatch` performs an outbound `fetch` without a timeout or abort signal. `flush()` awaits each batch serially, so an unresponsive Mixpanel endpoint can hold the integration job indefinitely.

## Code reference
- `worker/src/features/mixpanel/mixpanelClient.ts:42-59` — `flush` awaits every chunk before clearing the batch.
- `worker/src/features/mixpanel/mixpanelClient.ts:64-85` — Mixpanel `fetch` has no timeout.

## Reproduction
Configure a Mixpanel integration, or mock the import endpoint so it accepts the request and never responds, then run `MixpanelClient.flush()`.

## Expected behavior
The request should fail within a bounded time and let the queue's retry/backoff policy handle the batch.

## Actual behavior
`flush()` remains pending indefinitely and the batch is not cleared. The worker integration job cannot complete while the endpoint is hung.

## Why it matters
An external analytics outage can stall worker capacity and leave integration data pending indefinitely. The existing fix in #11988 addressed static job IDs and stalled-job handling, but not the unbounded HTTP request.

## Suggested fix
Add an abortable request timeout and define how timed-out batches are retried without duplicating already accepted events. Add a hanging-request regression test.

title: [bug] ClickHouse writer drops records permanently after max retries
body:
## Summary
When ClickHouse writes fail until the retry limit is reached, `ClickhouseWriter` permanently drops the records. The code contains an explicit TODO to replace this with a Redis dead-letter queue, but there is currently no replayable failure path.

## Code reference
- `worker/src/services/ClickhouseWriter/index.ts:532-571` — failed records are requeued only while `attempts < maxAttempts`; otherwise they are discarded and only metrics/logs are emitted.
- `worker/src/services/ClickhouseWriter/index.ts:544` — `TODO - Add to a dead letter queue in Redis rather than dropping`.
- `worker/src/services/ClickhouseWriter/__tests__/ClickhouseWriter.unit.test.ts:167-192` — the current test codifies dropping after max attempts.

## Reproduction
Make ClickHouse reject a queued batch until the configured maximum attempts are exhausted. Observe `langfuse.queue.clickhouse_writer.rows_dropped` and the error log, then verify that the records are absent from the queue and cannot be replayed.

## Expected behavior
Records that cannot be written after transient retries should be retained in a durable, replayable dead-letter path with enough context to reprocess them.

## Actual behavior
The records are discarded after the final retry. Observability reports the loss but cannot recover it.

## Why it matters
A temporary ClickHouse outage or poison batch can cause irreversible trace, observation, or score data loss.

## Suggested fix
Add a durable dead-letter queue/replay workflow, preserve the original payload and attempt metadata, and retain a test proving failed records are recoverable rather than dropped.

title: total_cost stays $0.00 on v4.6.0 for provided cost_details with mixed keys (input/output/cache_read, no total) even when the model IS in the pricing table
body:
## Environment

* Langfuse self-hosted **v4.6.0** (web + worker, `langfuse:4` tag, image built 2026-08-06)
* Ingestion via Langfuse SDK (Hermes Agent plugin) over OTel
* Model: `deepseek-v4-flash` (present on the observation, NOT in the pricing table by default)

## Summary

Per-type `cost_details` land and render, but the **derived total cost stays** `$0.00` when provided `cost_details` contain more than `{input, output}` and no explicit `total` key. This is a residual gap to langfuse/langfuse#15696/langfuse/langfuse#15717: that fix promotes provided costs for the *model-less* path, but the total-derivation logic still cannot total a mixed key set.

## Root cause (worker `IngestionService.calculateUsageCosts`)

When provided cost details are authoritative, the derived total is only computed as:

1. an explicit `total` key, **or**
2. sum of `input`+`output` **only if the key set is exactly** `{input, output}`

With a third key (e.g. `cache_read_input_tokens`) present, `finalTotalCost` is `undefined`, so `cost`/`totalCost` stay null and the UI renders `$0.00` even though per-type costs are present and correct.

## Empirical proof (reproduced live, then reverted)

1. Baseline: generation with model `deepseek-v4-flash` → `cost=null`, `totalCost=null`, per-type `costDetails` present (`{input, output, cache_read_input_tokens}`).
2. Added `deepseek-v4-flash` to `models` + a default `pricing_tiers` row + `prices` for input/output/cache_read (real rates) directly in Postgres, then cleared the Redis model-match cache (`LANGFUSE_MODEL_MATCH_NOT_FOUND` tokens).
3. Fired fresh LLM calls. ClickHouse ground truth:

   ```
   provided_model_name: deepseek-v4-flash
   model_id:            cm-empirical-deepseek-v4-flash   <-- matched our inserted row
   cost_details:        {input:0.00009716, output:0.00004172, cache_read_input_tokens:0.0010977792}
   total_cost:          0                                 <-- still zero
   ```
4. Reverted all DB rows and cache keys; verified baselin

title: Feature request: expose per-prompt label assignment history (opens up recoverability for label moves outside Enterprise)
body:
### Summary

Prompt labels behave like git tags — a label name points at exactly one version of a prompt at a time, and assigning it to a different version silently moves it. There is currently no way (outside Enterprise-tier audit logs) to inspect that history: when a label was assigned, what version it pointed at before a move, what version it points at now, who moved it, or why a release tag silently shifted.

This makes label recovery and forensic debuggability disproportionately expensive on non-Enterprise plans. For env-style labels (`production`, `staging`) the answer can sometimes be reconstructed from traces; for arbitrary release tags (`vX.Y.Z`) there is no native trail at all.

### Problem

* The `production` label is the default-fetch version in all SDKs; a silent move changes what an app runs without a noticeable event.
* Release-shaped labels (semver-like tags) are intended to be immutable point-in-time markers, but the API happily overwrites them — there is no client-side way to detect or revert a mistaken re-assignment without already knowing the prior version.
* The only native audit surface (`Prompt` audit resource covers `setLabel` and `promote` with before/after state — see the Audit Logs docs) is gated to Enterprise tiers (Hobby/Core/Pro: not available; Self-hosted: Enterprise edition only).

### Proposal

Per-prompt, per-label-name history, exposed via:

1. **UI**: a "Label history" tab/drawer on the prompt detail page — a chronological list of `[label, version, timestamp, actor]` rows.
2. **API**: a `GET /api/public/prompts/{name}/labels/{label}/history` endpoint (or extend the existing prompt-version response with a `labelHistory` array) returning the same rows.

Even a *last-N* or *time-window-limited* view (e.g. 90 days) would unblock recovery workflows on Hobby/Pro. Full Enterprise-grade retention can stay paid.

### Why this matters

* Labels are the only "what version ran in env X at time T" signal an operator has, but they are mutable w

title: bug: langfuse-cli "api dataset-items create" — "nullable" cannot be used without "type", input/expectedOutput/metadata unbindable
body:
## Bug
`langfuse-cli`'s generic `api dataset-items create` command cannot bind `input`, `expectedOutput`, or `metadata` at all — `--help` doesn't list them as flags, and forcing the call errors outright.

## Repro
```
npx langfuse-cli api dataset-items create --datasetName test --curl
```
```
error: "nullable" cannot be used without "type"
Run 'dataset-items create --help' to see available options.
```

## Expected
`dataset-items create` should accept `--input`, `--expectedOutput`, `--metadata` (as JSON strings) — these are the actual content of a dataset item, confirmed via `dataset-items list` (which returns them correctly) and the official docs (`/docs/evaluation/dataset-runs/datasets.md`), e.g.:
```json
{"input": {...}, "expectedOutput": {...}, "metadata": {...}}
```

## Root cause (guess)
Likely the request-body schema types these fields as `Any | None`, i.e. bare `"nullable": true` with no `"type"`. The CLI's flag-builder appears to require `type` whenever `nullable` is present, and fails closed instead of falling back to a generic JSON passthrough for untyped fields.

## Version
`langfuse-cli` 0.0.12 (via `npx`), self-hosted Langfuse server v3.218.0.

## Workaround used
Fell back to the Python SDK (`langfuse` 4.14.0) directly: `Langfuse.create_dataset_item(*, dataset_name, input=None, expected_output=None, metadata=None, ...)` has the exact same signature/semantics and works fine — this issue is scoped to the generic `api dataset-items create` CLI command, not the resource's write path in general (the SDK and `dataset-items list` both work correctly).

(Note: I originally tried to file this against `langfuse/langfuse-cli` directly, but issues are disabled on that repo, so filing here instead.)

title: [SDK][Python] NaN/Inf floats nested in a pydantic model serialize to invalid JSON (bare NaN/Infinity)
body:
**Which package?** Python SDK (`langfuse-python`)

**Describe the bug**

`EventSerializer` in `langfuse/_utils/serializer.py` converts non-finite floats (NaN/Inf) to JSON-safe string tokens (`"NaN"`, `"Infinity"`, `"-Infinity"`) along its manual dict/list recursion. But the `BaseModel` branch (`langfuse/_utils/serializer.py:132-139`) returns `obj.model_dump()` directly without recursing back through `default()`. As a result, a non-finite float nested inside a pydantic model bypasses the conversion, and Python's json C-encoder emits a bare `NaN`/`Infinity` token — invalid JSON that a strict `JSON.parse` (the ingestion server) rejects.

This is on the core tracing path: span `input`/`output`/`metadata` are serialized through this encoder via `langfuse/_client/attributes.py` `_serialize`. Any traced pydantic object carrying a NaN/Inf float (very common with ML/scoring payloads) produces an event body that fails ingestion.

**Runnable repro**

```python
import json
from pydantic import BaseModel
from langfuse._utils.serializer import EventSerializer

class Scores(BaseModel):
    confidence: float

encoded = EventSerializer().encode(Scores(confidence=float("nan")))
print(encoded)  # -> {"confidence": NaN}   (bare NaN, invalid JSON)

# Strict parse, as a JS/TS JSON.parse would do, fails:
json.loads(encoded, parse_constant=lambda t: (_ for _ in ()).throw(ValueError(t)))
# ValueError: NaN
```

Contrast with a plain dict `{"confidence": float("nan")}`, which correctly serializes to `{"confidence": "NaN"}`.

**Expected**

Nested non-finite floats inside pydantic models are converted to the same safe string tokens as everywhere else, producing strict-JSON-valid output.

**Environment:** `langfuse` Python SDK v4.14.x (current `main`).

body:
### Describe the bug

When configuring an LLM-as-a-Judge evaluator with a trace filter of metadata -> 'turn' -> contains -> '' (empty string), the setup preview behaves as a key-existence check: only traces that have a turn key in metadata are shown as matching.

However, once the evaluator is active, the worker enqueues and executes the evaluator on incoming traces that do not have the turn metadata key at all. The preview and the trigger path evaluate the same filter differently, so the filter that was validated visually in the wizard does not describe the population that actually gets judged (and billed).

# Expected behavior

Preview and worker should compile the filter identically. Whichever semantics is intended for contains "" on a metadata key (existence check vs. match-everything), both paths should agree — the preview is what users rely on to validate evaluator scope before spending eval tokens.

# Alternative

Please add a metadata key existence filter. 

### Steps to reproduce


1. Ingest traces via the OTel endpoint, some with metadata.turn = "<value>" set as a span/trace attribute, some without any turn key.
2. Create an evaluator (new traces) with filter: metadata → key turn → operator contains → value "" (empty string).
3. Observe the preview/matching sample in the wizard: only traces with the turn key appear. ✅
4. Activate the evaluator and ingest new traces without the turn key.

title: bug: v4 unified Tracing table cannot display trace total cost — root SPAN rows show $0.00
body: ### Describe the bug In the new unified **Tracing** table (v4 UI), there is no way to see the aggregated total cost of a trace at the row level. Our application (LangGraph agent) creates a root observation of type `SPAN` per conversation turn, with all LLM calls as nested `GENERATION` observations. With the default/root-observation view (`isRootObservation:true`, `type:SPAN`), the **Cost ($)** column shows the *observation-level* cost of the root span, which is always **$0.00** since spans cannot carry usage/cost. The actual trace cost only becomes visible after clicking into the trace detail view, where the aggregated total (Σ) is displayed correctly. In the previous Traces table (pre-v4 UI), the **Total Cost** column showed the trace-level aggregate per row, so we could scan/sort/export cost per trace directly from the list. That capability appears to be lost in the unified table: the column picker offers no trace-level cost column, only the per-observation cost. ### Steps to reproduce 1. Instrument an app where the root observation is a `SPAN` and LLM calls are child `GENERATION`s (e.g. any LangChain/LangGraph app via the Langfuse callback handler). 2. Open **Tracing** with filters `isRootObservation:true` + `type:SPAN` (one row per trace). 3. Enable the **Cost ($)** column. 4. Every row shows `$0.00`. 5. Open any row → trace detail correctly shows the aggregated cost (e.g. `Σ $0.051089`). Verified via the public API that the data is intact — this is purely a display/column gap: - `GET /api/public/traces/{id}` → `totalCost: 0.051089` - child generations carry `calculatedTotalCost` values summing to that total - root span observation → `calculatedTotalCost: 0`, as expected for a `SPAN` ### Langfus

title: bug(sdk-python): media is uploaded before masking runs — neither mask nor mask_otel_spans can prevent it
body:
### Describe the bug

## Summary

Media content is extracted and queued for upload *before* either masking hook can act on it, so neither `mask` nor `mask_otel_spans` can keep the bytes of an inline image, audio clip or document out of Langfuse. The masked span that ships afterwards carries only a `@@@langfuseMedia:...` reference, which reads as if masking worked.

The ordering itself is deliberate — `_process_media_attributes()` runs ahead of `_apply_mask_otel_spans()` in `LangfuseSpanExporter.export()`, and `test_mask_otel_spans_receives_post_media_batch_and_applies_sparse_patch` pins it. What I don't think is intended is the consequence: `mask_otel_spans` is documented as the export-stage hook for exactly this problem, and it is structurally unable to prevent a media upload.

The sharpest case is the failure path. The docstring says:

> If the hook raises or returns an invalid batch result, Langfuse drops the whole export batch.

That is a fail-closed guarantee, and it doesn't hold for media. When the hook raises, the span batch is dropped as documented — and the media bytes are uploaded anyway.

## Expected behavior

One of:

* media extraction runs after the masking hooks, so a redacted attribute never produces an upload; or
* media uploads enqueued from a batch are discarded when that batch is dropped, so "drops the whole export batch" means all of it; or
* at minimum, the `mask` / `mask_otel_spans` docs state plainly that neither hook covers media content, and that inline media must be stripped before it reaches the SDK.

## Actual behavior

Span attributes are masked correctly. The media bytes behind them are queued for upload with their original content, including when the batch that produced them is dropped.

The legacy `mask` hook doesn't help either, though for a different reason: media is extracted at attribute-creation time, so `mask` is handed a `LangfuseMedia` object rather than the `data:` URI. A string-based masking function — the shape in every ex

title: bug(playground): tools and structured output are lost when round-tripping between the playground and saved prompts
body: ### Describe the bug Tool definitions and structured output schemas have no path through saved prompts. They live in playground state only, so they are dropped in both directions: - **playground -> prompt:** "Save as prompt" / "Save as new prompt version" carries over the messages, but never writes tools or the structured output schema into `prompt.config`. - **prompt -> playground:** opening a prompt in the playground returns only messages, so even a prompt whose `config` already contains a schema written by hand, or by an SDK following the [Prompt Config docs](https://langfuse.com/docs/prompt-management/features/config). It opens with the schema panel empty. The net effect is that any prompt iterated on in the playground silently loses its tools and schema the moment it is saved, which makes the playground unusable for the tool-calling and structured-output workflows it advertises. ### Steps to reproduce 1. Open the playground, define a tool and a structured output schema. 2. Click **Save as prompt** and save. 3. Open the saved prompt and check its **Config**. No `tools`, no schema. Second path, no playground involved: 1. Create a prompt whose config is the `response_format` example straight from the [Prompt Config docs](https://langfuse.com/docs/prompt-management/features/config#structured-outputs). 2. Open it in the playground — the structured output panel is empty, even though the schema is right there in the config. ### Langfuse

title: Feature request: git-style branching, merging & approval gates for Prompt Management
body:
## Context

We run Langfuse Prompt Management in production for a multi-prompt LLM application (tracing + prompts together). For us prompts are engineering artifacts coupled to structured-output schemas and tool contracts, so iterating on them is a first-class activity — done by engineers and non-engineers side by side. The linear version + label model serves incremental iteration well; this request is about what it can't express.

## The gaps we hits

### 1. No branching for parallel experimentation

When a prompt needs a fundamentally different approach (restructured instructions, different strategy — not a tweak), we want 2–4 competing rewrites evaluated side by side against the same dataset. Today the only options are:

- linear versions — serial, cluttering the one lineage with dead ends, or
- separate prompt names (`task--attempt-b`) with manual copy-back — loses the relationship and history.

What we'd want: fork any version into a branch, iterate in the branch, run experiments per branch, merge the winner back — with the losing branches kept inspectable. This is the same ask as #11997 (I know it's closed as not planned — hoping a more detailed pain picture and a concrete shape can reopen the conversation).

### 2. Promotion has a record, not a gate

Version history tells you *what* changed; nothing *prevents* a bad version from reaching the `production` label. On small teams the same person edits, evaluates, and promotes — i.e., pure self-review, at exactly the layer where behavior regressions are most common for us (prompt changes, not code). A lightweight gate — "open change request / PR analogue → approval required before a label can move to the merged version" — would close this.

### 3. The GitHub integrations are one-way

Repository Dispatch and the sync-server pattern give git *visibility* into prompt changes, but nothing flows back, so git can't serve as the review/audit surface. Teams that want PR-style review end up building bespoke CLIs (fetch → l

langfuse-openeval-adapter: convert Langfuse datasets/experiment results to/from EvalPort
body:
Hi Langfuse team — I maintain [EvalPort](https://github.com/adhabnr-ux/evalport), an open interchange format for portable LLM evaluation test cases, graders, suites, and results (~20 framework adapters so far, including LangSmith, MLflow, Ragas, Braintrust). Built and shipped a standalone adapter for Langfuse: [langfuse-openeval-adapter](https://github.com/adhabnr-ux/evalport/tree/main/adapters/langfuse-openeval-adapter).

```python
from langfuse import Langfuse
from langfuse_openeval_adapter import to_openeval, from_openeval, experiment_result_to_openeval

lf = Langfuse()
dataset = lf.get_dataset("geo_science_eval")

suite = to_openeval(dataset.items, suite_id="geo_science_eval")   # -> spec-valid EvalPort suite

rows = from_openeval(suite)   # -> usable directly as run_experiment()'s `data` argument
result = lf.run_experiment(name="geo_science_eval", data=rows,
                            task=lambda item, **_: my_app(item["input"]),
                            evaluators=[correctness_evaluator])

result_set = experiment_result_to_openeval(result, suite_id="geo_science_eval", run_id=result.run_name)
```

A couple of design details I put real thought into, in case they're useful context:

- `to_openeval()` also accepts plain `{"input", "expected_output", "metadata"}` dicts — the same shape `run_experiment(data=...)` already accepts for ad-hoc data — so a stored dataset isn't required.
- The full original dataset item (`id`, `status`, `dataset_id`, `dataset_name`, `source_trace_id`, ...) round-trips losslessly under `metadata["langfuse"]["item"]`, so nothing Langfuse-specific is lost going Langfuse → EvalPort → Langfuse.
- `Evaluation.value`'s three real shapes (`BOOLEAN`, `NUMERIC`, `CATEGORICAL`) are each handled on their own terms rather than force-fit into one rule — numeric scores get clamped into EvalPort's required `[0,1]` range with the raw value preserved, categorical labels get `score: null` (no fabricated number) with an explicit small set of affirmative

body:
### Describe the bug

In an **async** LangChain/LangGraph run, `LangchainCallbackHandler` lands `user_id` /
`session_id` / `tags` / `trace_name` on the **root span only**. Every child observation —
including the `GENERATION`s that carry the cost — is exported with no `user.id`,
no `session.id` and no `langfuse.trace.tags`.

The same code path in a **sync** run attributes every observation correctly.

This matters much more on v4 than it did on v3: v4 aggregates over the wide observations
table, so an unattributed generation is an unattributed cost. Concretely, the built-in
"cost by user" dashboard tile reports ~100% of spend under an unknown user for any async
app, and filtering the observations table by a trace tag returns only root spans.

The handler already does the right thing — `on_chain_start` builds a
`propagate_attributes(...)` context manager and enters it
([`CallbackHandler.py`](https://github.com/langfuse/langfuse-python/blob/main/langfuse/langchain/CallbackHandler.py), the
`if parent_run_id is None:` block). The problem is *where* that context lives.

`LangchainCallbackHandler` is a sync `BaseCallbackHandler` and does not set
`run_inline`, so `run_inline` is `False`. LangChain's `AsyncCallbackManager` therefore
dispatches every callback as (`langchain_core/callbacks/manager.py`,
`_ahandle_event_for_handler`):

```python
await asyncio.get_event_loop().run_in_executor(
    None,
    functools.partial(copy_context().run, event, *args, **kwargs),
)
```

`copy_context()` is taken in the event loop and the callback runs against that **copy** in
a worker thread. The `otel_context_api.attach(context)` performed inside
`_propagate_attributes` mutates the copy, which is discarded the moment the executor
callable returns. Every later callback (`on_chat_model_start`, `on_tool_start`, …) gets a
fresh copy of the caller's context that never saw the attach, and
`LangfuseSpanProcessor.on_start` → `_get_propagated_attributes_from_context(context)`
finds nothing. Only th

title: feat(redis): support Microsoft Entra ID authentication
body:
## Problem

Langfuse can only authenticate to Redis with a static password (`REDIS_AUTH`) or a connection string. On Azure this blocks two common deployments:

- **Azure Managed Redis caches with access keys disabled**, where Microsoft Entra ID is the only accepted authentication method. Entra is enabled by default on newly created AMR caches, so this affects new deployments out of the box.
- **Environments with a no-static-secrets policy**, where a long-lived cache password in the environment is not permitted.

The hard part is not acquiring a token — it is that Entra credentials are short-lived. The server drops connections when a token expires, so the client must re-`AUTH` on live connections before expiry. ioredis has no credential-provider hook (redis/ioredis#2022 is still open) and Microsoft's `@redis/entraid` only supports node-redis, so this has to be handled in Langfuse.

## Proposal

Introduce a credential-provider seam in `packages/shared/src/server/redis/` rather than special-casing Azure.

`createNewRedisInstance` asks a provider for credentials instead of reading `REDIS_AUTH` directly:

- The **default provider is static** and behaviourally identical to today — no timers, no connection registry, no re-authentication.
- A **rotating provider** handles acquisition, renewal and re-`AUTH` on live connections.

Everything auth-specific reduces to one factory returning an `@azure/identity` `TokenCredential`, which covers managed identity, workload identity, service principal (secret or certificate) and the local Azure CLI credential from a single code path. The same machinery would later cover AWS ElastiCache IAM auth, which may be the more widely requested case.

Gated behind `REDIS_AUTH_MODE`, defaulting to `password`, so existing deployments are untouched.

## Questions for maintainers

1. **New dependency.** This needs `@azure/identity`. Langfuse currently authenticates Azure Blob with `StorageSharedKeyCredential` (`StorageService.ts:375`), so there is n

body:
## Describe the bug

When the OpenAI Responses API reports GPT-5.6 cache-write usage, the official `@langfuse/openai` wrapper persists it as `input_cache_write_tokens`, but the Langfuse GPT-5.6 pricing definitions do not contain a price for that usage key. As a result, the tokens are present in `usageDetails` while their cost is silently omitted from `costDetails` and `totalCost`.

The mismatch is internal to Langfuse:

1. OpenAI returns `usage.input_tokens_details.cache_write_tokens`.
2. [`parseUsageDetails`](<https://github.com/langfuse/langfuse-js/blob/main/packages/openai/src/parseOpenAI.ts>) prefixes Responses API input detail keys with `input_`, producing `input_cache_write_tokens`.
3. The current [`gpt-5.6-sol` pricing definition](<https://github.com/langfuse/langfuse/blob/main/worker/src/constants/default-model-prices.json>) prices `input_cache_creation` and `cache_write_tokens`, but not `input_cache_write_tokens`.
4. Usage-to-price matching therefore leaves this positive usage bucket unpriced.

Expected behavior: `input_cache_write_tokens` should be recognized as an alias of `input_cache_creation` and priced at the GPT-5.6 cache-write rate. OpenAI documents cache writes at 1.25x the uncached input rate. For GPT-5.6 Sol requests above 272K input tokens, this is $12.50 per million tokens.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Wrap the OpenAI Node SDK with `observeOpenAI` from `@langfuse/openai@5.10.0`.
2. Send a Responses API request using `gpt-5.6-sol` that produces non-zero `input_tokens_details.cache_write_tokens`.
3. Retrieve the generation through `GET /api/public/v2/observations` with the `usage` field group.
4. Observe that `usageDetails.input_cache_write_tokens` is positive, but `costDetails.input_cache_write_tokens` is absent.

title: Feature: label filter for GitHub Repository Dispatch prompt automation
body:
## Problem

The **GitHub Repository Dispatch** prompt automation (Prompts → Automations) currently fires on every prompt-version event, with only a prompt-name filter. Teams using labels as their promotion lifecycle (e.g. `production` vs `staging`/draft) get a dispatch for **every iteration of every prompt**, and must filter inside the GitHub workflow:

```yaml
jobs:
  sync:
    if: contains(github.event.client_payload.prompt.labels, 'production')
```

(from the docs' own example: https://langfuse.com/docs/prompt-management/features/github-integration)

This works, but:
- Every non-matching event still consumes a GitHub Actions run (runner allocation + checkout before the job-level `if` can skip) — noisy run history and wasted minutes for active teams
- The filter is re-implemented in every consumer workflow instead of declared once at the source

## Proposal

Add a **label filter** to the automation configuration, alongside the existing prompt-name filter:

- UI: multi-select or free-text label(s) in automation settings
- Semantics: dispatch only when the saved version carries any (or all, configurable) of the selected labels — e.g. select `production` → only production-labelled saves dispatch
- `labels` is already in the webhook payload, so this is a payload-side predicate before the HTTP POST — no new plumbing

Webhooks have the same shape (event-type filter only); landing the filter there too would benefit both integration styles.

## Workaround (current)

Job-level `if: contains(github.event.client_payload.prompt.labels, '<label>')` in the workflow — documented pattern, just pays a runner allocation per filtered event.

title: feat(trace): add a flame graph view to visualize where time goes in a trace
body:
## Summary

Flame graphs — Brendan Gregg's standard visualization for performance profiling — answer "where does the time actually go?" in a single glance: x-axis = time, bar width = duration, y-axis = nesting depth. LLM/agent traces are getting deep and wide (a single agent run contains dozens of nested LLM calls, tool calls, retrievals, and sub-agent handoffs), yet none of the major LLM observability platforms (LangSmith, Phoenix, Helicone, Datadog LLM Observability, …) offer a flame graph view today.

I'd like to propose adding a **Flame view** to the trace detail page, alongside the existing Tree / Timeline / Graph / Log views.

## Why it's useful

1. **Hotspot detection** — bar width = duration, so the most expensive span (slowest LLM call, slowest tool) is visible by area at a glance. In a waterfall you have to sum durations across rows mentally.
2. **Parallelism & cost peaks** — agents execute spans concurrently (parallel tool calls, LangGraph branches, MoA fan-outs). A flame view stacks parallel spans vertically, making "windows where many things are burning time — and tokens — at once" immediately visible. Since Langfuse already tracks token usage/cost per observation, bars could optionally be colored by cost.
3. **Nesting depth abuse** — y-axis encodes depth, so pathological nesting (agent → sub-agent → tool → LLM → …) shows up as tall columns instead of subtle indentation in a tree.
4. **(v2, later)** **Aggregation & regression** — flame graphs are the standard for comparing runs; env/release tags already exist on traces, making a future "compare two traces" view natural.

## Relationship to the existing Timeline

The Timeline (waterfall) view already lays spans on a time axis — one row per node in tree order. A flame view is the same data re-projected: **y = nesting depth instead of row order**, spans rendered as stacked bars. The existing `TraceTimelineV2` infrastructure (`layout()`, `viewTransform`, `timeCompression`) appears largely reusable.

```

title: bug: Basic auth resolves API keys by secret-key hash only; public-key mismatch is a warning, not a rejection
body:
### Describe the bug

On the public-API **Basic auth** path, an API key is resolved solely by the hash of the *secret*
key. The submitted *public* key (the Basic-auth username) is not an authentication factor: when it
does not match the key that owns the secret, the server logs a warning and **authenticates the
request anyway**.

Version observed: **v4.11.0**, self-hosted, `events_only`. The relevant code is present on `main`
as well.

## Where

`web/src/features/public-api/server/apiAuth.ts`, Basic-auth branch. The key is resolved via
`createShaHash(secretKey, salt)` against `fastHashedSecretKey` (falling back to a Postgres lookup
by the same hash). After resolution, a public-key mismatch is handled as:

```ts
// The API key is resolved via the hash of the secret key, so the
// submitted public key may not belong to it, e.g. after a partial
// credential rotation on the client.
if (publicKey !== finalApiKey.publicKey) {
  logger.warn(`Public key mismatch on basic auth: ...`);
}
// ...proceeds to return { validKey: true, ... }
```

There is no `throw` between the warning and the successful return, so a mismatch does not reject.

## Suggested fix

Reject on public-key mismatch (401) rather than warning. If the current tolerance was intentional
(the code comment cites partial client-side rotation), gate the strict behaviour behind a config
flag and default it on, and/or surface in the docs that until then the secret key is the sole
authentication factor and public-key deletion does not revoke a shared secret.

### Steps to reproduce

1. In one project, create key A `(pkA, skA)` and key B `(pkB, skB)`.
2. Send a Basic-auth request with username `pkA` and password `skB`
   (`Authorization: Basic base64("pkA:skB")`) to any public-API endpoint.
   → **200**, authenticated as key B. Only a warning is logged.
3. Delete key A in the UI (or via API).
4. Repeat step 2 with `(pkA, skB)`.
   → still **200**, still authenticated as key B.

### Langfuse Cloud or self-hosted?

Self

title: Opt-in tamper-evident experiments: lock evaluator + threshold + items hash before the run (working example included)
body:
Per CONTRIBUTING, opening this for discussion before any code.

**Problem.** A Langfuse experiment records what happened — task outputs, item evaluations, run-level aggregates. What no experiment record can say about itself is what the bar *was* before the run: which evaluator decides the claim, what aggregate counts as success, which items (by content, not by dataset name) the claim is about. Each of those is chosen by whoever publishes the number, and can be adjusted after the aggregate is known. Teams quoting experiment results as CI gates or compliance evidence currently have no way to show a third party that the pass bar predates the score.

**Proposal (opt-in, zero default change).** A small pre-registration hook on the experiment flow: before the run, a manifest binds the run-level evaluation name, comparator + threshold, a SHA-256 over the canonical JSON of the items, and the seed — locked to a SHA-256 digest. After the run, verification checks the run-level aggregate against the locked bar. Anyone can verify offline with the manifest text and any SHA-256 implementation; no service involved, including ours — deliberately, since a lock that depended on any platform (ours or yours) would be weaker evidence.

**Working example, not just an ask:** https://github.com/studio-11-co/falsify/tree/main/examples/langfuse

It uses the Python SDK's own machinery rather than imitating it — tasks and evaluators through the same normalization `run_experiment` uses, real `ExperimentItemResult` and `Evaluation` objects, the aggregate as a run-level evaluator in exactly the documented shape — verified against langfuse 4.14.4 from PyPI in a clean environment, all three verdicts exercised (PASS / FAIL / TAMPERED-after-edit). The platform upload is the one step the demo doesn't exercise, and the README says so.

The manifest format is PRML, openly specified (CC BY 4.0, https://spec.falsify.dev), with test vectors and four byte-equivalent reference implementations; it is also prop

title: bug: Gemini thinking tokens included in Σ total but not in cost → under-reporting
body:
Describe the bug

We are using gemini-2.5-flash in production and see a consistent gap between the cost Langfuse reports and the cost on the Google Cloud / AI Studio API billing console — Langfuse is always lower than what Google actually charges us.

After comparing traces, we believe the cause is that Langfuse does not include Gemini's thinking tokens (thoughts_token_count) in its cost calculation, even though it does include them in the displayed total token count (Σ). Since Google bills thinking tokens at the output rate, dropping them from the cost makes every reasoning-heavy Gemini call cheaper in Langfuse than on the invoice.

This looks like the same underlying issue as the earlier report about Gemini cost vs. Google Cloud billing. Attaching our screenshots as additional confirmation, with the specific behavior isolated.

For the GPT model, input + output = Σ total for every observation, e.g. 949 → 1,239 (Σ 2,188) where 949 + 1,239 = 2,188. The cost is applied to all output tokens, so Langfuse's number matches the bill. Nothing is missed here because reasoning tokens (if any) are already folded into the output count.

For gemini-2.5-flash, input + visible output ≠ Σ total. The Σ is larger because it includes thoughts_token_count, but those thinking tokens are not priced. Example rows (input → visible output (Σ total), cost):

  • section:overview — 4,773 → 1,329 (Σ 10,872), $0.004754
  • section:lesson — 10,381 → 5,182 (Σ 19,447), $0.016069
  • section:support — 4,682 → 2,671 (Σ 12,777), $0.008

title: bug: unbounded ClickHouse Docker log can exhaust self-hosted server after ENOSPC
body:
### Describe the bug

The default self-hosted Docker Compose configuration does not bound the ClickHouse container logs. With Docker's default `json-file` logging driver, stdout/stderr can grow without rotation.

On a self-hosted instance, the host filesystem reached `ENOSPC`. ClickHouse could no longer write or rotate its internal files under `/var/log/clickhouse-server` and repeatedly emitted the following failure to stderr:

```text
Cannot log message in OwnAsyncSplitChannel channel:
Poco::Exception. Code: 1000, File access error:
/var/log/clickhouse-server/clickhouse-server.log
Poco::RotateBySizeStrategy::mustRotate(...)
```

Docker captured this output in the container's unbounded `*-json.log`. That file reached **89.1 GiB**, the 244 GiB root filesystem reached **100% / 0 bytes available**, and even `docker exec` / `docker run` began failing with `no space left on device`.

Expected: the bundled self-hosting path should either bound container logs or prominently require host-level Docker log rotation, so a ClickHouse logging failure cannot consume the entire host filesystem.

This is related to, but distinct from, #13123:

- #13123 concerns ClickHouse system tables stored inside `/var/lib/clickhouse`.
- This report concerns the outer Docker `json-file` log under `/var/lib/docker/containers` and the feedback loop after the filesystem fills.

Both occurred on this instance: ClickHouse `system` tables occupied **22.87 GiB**, while the Langfuse `default` database occupied **487.20 MiB**.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Deploy Langfuse using the default self-hosted `docker-compose.yml` and Docker's default `json-file` logging driver.
2. Do not configure daemon-level or per-service log rotation.
3. On a disposable test host, exhaust the filesystem until ClickHouse cannot write or rotate `/var/log/clickhouse-server/clickhouse-server.log`.
4. Observe repeated `OwnAsyncSplitChannel` / `RotateBySizeStrategy::mustRotate` errors on ClickHouse stderr.
5. Observe the ClickHouse

body:
The v3 -> v4 guide states, under **Rollback and safety**:

> The v4 schema migrations are additive (new tables only). While you run the
> `legacy` or `dual` write mode, the old `traces`/`observations` tables keep
> receiving all data, so you can roll the server back to the latest v3 release
> without data loss.

Both halves of that appear to be inaccurate; we hit the second one during a
rollback rehearsal. Filing as one issue since they share a root cause.

## 1. The migrations are not additive

v4.10.0 drops seven tables and three enum types.

ClickHouse:

| Migration | Statement |
| --- | --- |
| `0044_drop_event_log.up.sql` | `DROP TABLE IF EXISTS event_log` |
| `0045_drop_project_environments.up.sql` | `DROP TABLE IF EXISTS project_environments` |
| `0046_drop_dataset_run_items.up.sql` | `DROP TABLE IF EXISTS dataset_run_items` |

PostgreSQL:

| Migration | Statement |
| --- | --- |
| `20260723150000_drop_legacy_tracing_tables` | `DROP TABLE traces`, `observations`, `scores` + `DROP TYPE ObservationType`, `ObservationLevel`, `ScoreSource` |
| `20260723124010_drop_dataset_run_items_table` | `DROP TABLE dataset_run_items` |

The ClickHouse `traces`/`observations`/`scores` tables do survive, so the intent
behind the sentence holds. But "new tables only" is what a reader checks their
backup strategy against, and it is not what the migrations do.

`20260723150000_drop_legacy_tracing_tables` opens with:

```sql
-- The traces, observations and scores tables were superseded by their
-- ClickHouse counterparts in v3. Their contents were copied over by the
-- 20241024_* background migrations, which must have completed (on the latest
-- v3 release) before upgrading to v4.

That condition does not appear anywhere in the upgrade guide. Grepping the page
for `20241024`, `must have completed`, or any equivalent prerequisite returns

title: [Shared] score repository pagination drops offset=0
body:
### Summary

The score repository omits the requested `LIMIT/OFFSET` clause when `offset` is `0`, because the trace, session, and experiment query builders use a truthiness check (`limit && offset`). This makes the first page ignore the caller-provided limit.

### Reproduction

Call any of these repository functions with a non-zero limit and `offset: 0`:

- `getScoresForTraces`
- `getScoresForSessions`
- `getScoresForExperiments`

The generated ClickHouse query does not contain `LIMIT {limit: Int32} OFFSET {offset: Int32}`, so the response is not bounded by the requested page size. A positive offset does include the clause.

### Expected behavior

`offset: 0` is a valid first-page offset and should apply the same pagination as any other defined offset. The guard should check for `undefined` rather than truthiness for both `limit` and `offset`.

### Scope

The defect is isolated to the three score repository query builders in `packages/shared/src/server/repositories/scores.ts`; deterministic mocked-query tests can cover all three paths without a ClickHouse service.

title: bug: public key is dropped from the "No key found for public key" log line
body:
### Describe the bug

`ApiAuthService.verifyAuthHeaderAndReturnScope` logs the rejected public key at [`apiAuth.ts:116`](https://github.com/langfuse/langfuse/blob/main/web/src/features/public-api/server/apiAuth.ts#L116):

```ts
logger.error("No key found for public key", publicKey);
```

`publicKey` is a **string**, so winston routes it to the `SPLAT` symbol instead of merging it into `info`. The format chain in [`packages/shared/src/server/logger.ts`](https://github.com/langfuse/langfuse/blob/main/packages/shared/src/server/logger.ts) contains no `winston.format.splat()`, and the message has no `%s` placeholder — so the value never reaches the output, in **either** format:

- `LANGFUSE_LOG_FORMAT=text` — the `printf` at logger.ts:35-38 emits only `timestamp`, `level`, `message` (+ `stack`), dropping all metadata.
- default JSON — `winston.format.json()` serializes enumerable string keys only; `SPLAT` is a symbol.

The operator-visible result is `error  No key found for public key` with no indication of *which* key was rejected, and there is no other server-side signal: the repeat-request path short-circuits at the `API_KEY_NON_EXISTENT` negative cache (apiAuth.ts:315-317) and logs nothing beyond the generic `Error verifying auth header: Invalid credentials`. Identifying the misconfigured client then requires request-level logging at the ingress/proxy, which self-hosted deployments often don't have for that host.

By contrast, [`apiAuth.ts:135`](https://github.com/langfuse/langfuse/blob/main/web/src/features/public-api/server/apiAuth.ts#L135) — the wrong-secret-for-a-known-public-key case — interpolates, and *does* surface the key:

```ts
logger.debug(`Old key is invalid: ${publicKey}`);
```

So the intent to log the key clearly exists; L116 just uses a call shape winston discards.

The same call shape appears three more times in the same file, with the same effect:

| Line | Call | Dropped value |

title: feat: add OrcaRouter as a first-class LLM connection adapter
body:
### Feature request: OrcaRouter as a first-class LLM connection adapter

**Is your feature request related to a problem?**
[OrcaRouter](https://www.orcarouter.ai) is an OpenAI-compatible chat gateway (API base `https://api.orcarouter.ai/v1`, key prefix `sk-orca-`). Langfuse's LLM connections already support OpenAI-compatible endpoints through the `openai` adapter with a custom base URL, but there is no named adapter for OrcaRouter — users must manually fill in the base URL and model namespace.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
Add a first-class `orcarouter` LLM connection adapter that mirrors the OpenAI adapter surface:
- Adapter name `orcarouter`, default base URL `https://api.orcarouter.ai/v1`
- Default models: `orcarouter/auto`, `orcarouter/fusion`, `orcarouter/fusion-flash`, `orcarouter/fusion-mini`
- Full support in the playground model picker, eval/experiment execution, the public `/api/public/llm-connections` API, and the "New LLM Connection" form (adapter dropdown, base URL prefill, advanced settings).

It also runs gateway-level, zero-trust security for AI agents on the same endpoint — screening every prompt/response and governing every tool call on a default-deny basis, with no application code changes.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
Using the existing `openai` adapter with a custom base URL, which works but requires manual setup and exposes no named OrcaRouter option.

**Additional context**
I have a working implementation ready to submit as a PR (branch `add-orcarouter-provider` on my fork). This issue is to align with the contributing guideline that significant changes be discussed first.

Disclosure: I'm an engineer on the OrcaRouter team.

title: MCP: merge getPrompt / getPromptUnresolved into one tool and default to unresolved
body:
## Summary

The Langfuse MCP server exposes two prompt-fetch tools:

- `getPrompt` (`resolve: true`) — returns prompt content with **resolved dependencies** (referenced snippets interpolated inline).
- `getPromptUnresolved` (`resolve: false`) — returns raw content with **dependency tags intact** (e.g. `@@@langfusePrompt:name=...@@@`).

(See `web/src/features/mcp/features/prompts/tools/getPrompt.ts` and `getPromptUnresolved.ts`.)

Suggestion: **merge these into a single tool**, and make **unresolved the default** — e.g. a single `getPrompt` with an optional `resolve` boolean defaulting to `false`.

## Motivation

When using the MCP server with an AI coding agent, the agent almost always wants the **unresolved** version, but naturally reaches for the more generically/authoritatively named `getPrompt`. That tool silently interpolates referenced snippets, which:

- **Breaks/obscures snippet composition** — the agent sees inlined content instead of the `@@@langfusePrompt:...@@@` dependency tags, so it cannot reason about or safely edit the referenced snippets.
- **Causes edits against resolved output** rather than the actual source prompt, corrupting the composition when the agent writes a new version.

Because `getPrompt` is the obvious default name, the resolving behavior gets selected by accident. Splitting the behavior across two similarly-named tools makes this failure mode very easy to hit.

## Proposal

Prefer one of:

1. Collapse into a single tool (`getPrompt`) with an optional `resolve` parameter that **defaults to `false`** (unresolved), deprecating `getPromptUnresolved`; or
2. Keep a single tool returning unresolved content by default, resolving only when explicitly requested.

The `resolve` plumbing already exists (see #10951), so this is largely a matter of collapsing the two tool definitions and flipping the default.

### Considerations

- This changes the default behavior, so it's a behavioral breaking change for existing MCP consumers relying on resolved

### Describe the bug

The managed entries for `gpt-5.4-mini` and `gpt-5.4-nano` carry no price for the reasoning bucket. Reasoning tokens are ingested and stored, but since price matching is exact by usage key and `output` excludes any `output_*` value, they are multiplied by nothing — every generation that reasons is under-costed by `reasoning tokens x output rate`.

Current managed prices, via `GET /api/public/models`:

```
gpt-5.4       input 2.5e-06   input_cached_tokens 2.5e-07   input_cache_read 2.5e-07   cache_read_input_tokens 2.5e-07
              output 1.5e-05  output_reasoning 1.5e-05      output_reasoning_tokens 1.5e-05   reasoning_tokens 1.5e-05

gpt-5.4-mini  input 7.5e-07   input_cached_tokens 7.5e-08   input_cache_read 7.5e-08   cache_read_input_tokens 7.5e-08
              output 4.5e-06  -- no reasoning key --

gpt-5.4-nano  input 2e-07     input_cached_tokens 2e-08     input_cache_read 2e-08     cache_read_input_tokens 2e-08
              output 1.25e-06 -- no reasoning key --
```

The base `gpt-5.4` entry has all three reasoning aliases at its output rate. The two smaller models of the same family have none, which looks like an oversight rather than a decision.

title: bug: entrypoint.sh prints misleading "CLICKHOUSE_PASSWORD ... not URL-encoded" hint on every ClickHouse migration failure
body: ### Describe the bug When ClickHouse migrations fail for **any** reason, `web/entrypoint.sh` always prints: ``` Applying clickhouse migrations failed. Common causes: 1. The database is unavailable or unreachable. 2. CLICKHOUSE_PASSWORD contains special characters that are not URL-encoded. ``` The "Common cause 2" line is emitted **unconditionally** (`web/entrypoint.sh:121`). The accompanying detailed `HINT` from `check_clickhouse_password()` is correctly conditional (it only prints when `CLICKHOUSE_PASSWORD` actually contains `& = # ? % + @ space`), but because cause 2 is listed as a generic "common cause" on *every* failure, users with a perfectly valid alphanumeric password are misled into believing their `CLICKHOUSE_PASSWORD` is the problem — when the real cause is usually something else (a dirty `schema_migrations` state, an unreachable DB, an interrupted migration, etc.). The existing issues about `CLICKHOUSE_PASSWORD` (#13314, #12077) are about the *real* special-character bug, which is already fixed. This issue is specifically about the **misleading framing** of the hint when the password is fine. ### Real-world case Self-hosted via the official `docker-compose.yml` with `CLICKHOUSE_PASSWORD=password` (no special characters). The web container crashed on boot and the logs prominently showed the "Common cause 2" line. The actual error, printed *above* the hint, was: ``` error: Dirty database version 1. Fix and force version. ``` A previous `docker compose up` had been interrupted (containers exited 137) while ClickHouse migration 1 was applying, leaving `schema_migrations` at `version=1, dirty=1`. Auth to ClickHouse was succeeding the whole time — the password was never the issue. The "common cause 2" framing sent me down the wrong path (password / URL-encoding) before I read the real `Dirty database version` line ab

title: Corrupted evaluation-rule filter prevents disabling or deleting an active rule via public API
body:
### Describe the bug

A migrated/v2 evaluation rule with two LLM-as-a-judge assignments is actively producing scores, but every public API operation on that rule fails with HTTP 500:

```json
{"message":"Evaluation rule filter is corrupted","code":"internal_error"}
```

This includes:

- `GET /api/public/unstable/evaluation-rules/{id}`
- `PATCH ...` with only `{"enabled": false}`
- `PATCH ...` with a complete valid replacement observation filter plus `enabled: false`
- `DELETE ...`
- list, because it includes the same rule

A separate rule in the same project with a normal `isRootObservation = true` filter can be read and disabled successfully, so auth/project access is not the issue.

### Impact

There is no public-API escape hatch to stop a live rule once its stored filter no longer passes the new public adapter. The rule continues invoking judges and incurring cost. Even DELETE is blocked.

### Likely cause

On current `main`, `updatePublicEvaluationRule` calls `toApiWritableV2EvaluationRule(existing)` before applying the replacement input, and `deletePublicEvaluationRule` does the same before deleting. That serialisation reaches `toApiFilters()` and throws before either mutation can run:

- `web/src/features/evals/server/unstable-public-api/evaluation-rule-service.ts`
- `web/src/features/evals/server/unstable-public-api/adapters.ts`

### Expected behavior

At minimum, disabling and deleting should remain possible for a malformed legacy/migrated rule. A full filter replacement should also be able to repair it without first parsing the old filter. Possible approaches:

1. let `PATCH {enabled:false}` and DELETE mutate from the stored record without public serialisation first;
2. when a complete replacement filter is provided, do not derive `nextFilter` from `existingPublic`;
3. return a degraded read representation plus a corruption warning instead of making the resource unmanageable.

### Environment

- Langfuse Cloud
- Public API/CLI schema 4.10.0
- Observed 2026

title: bug(chatml): legacy OpenAI outputs with empty `completion` lose the `reasoning` value during normalization
body:
## bug(chatml): legacy OpenAI outputs with empty `completion` lose the `reasoning` value during normalization

### Problem

For a generation whose output object is `{"completion": "", "reasoning": "..."}` (a legitimate shape for reasoning models that produce reasoning but deliberately emit no assistant text), the observation panel's pretty view omits the reasoning block. The data itself is intact: fetching the same trace via the public API returns the full reasoning string, so this is purely a rendering issue in the chatml normalization pipeline.

Both prior PRs (#15370 `fix/reasoning-block-empty-completion` and #16158 `agent/fix-empty-completion-reasoning`) attempted this fix and were closed without merging. The diagnosis they shared is correct, but the fix needs to live in a different place.

### Root cause

`packages/shared/src/utils/IORepresentation/chatML/types.ts` defines `BaseChatMlMessageSchema` with the following fields:

```ts
{
  role: z.string().optional(),
  name: z.string().optional(),
  content: z.union([...]).nullish(),
  audio: OpenAIOutputAudioSchema.optional(),
  additional_kwargs: z.record(z.string(), z.any()).optional(),
  tools: z.array(ToolDefinitionSchema).optional(),
  tool_calls: z.array(ToolCallSchema).optional(),
  tool_call_id: z.string().optional(),
  // Thinking/reasoning content from models
  thinking: z.array(ThinkingContentPartSchema).optional(),
  redacted_thinking: z.array(RedactedThinkingContentPartSchema).optional(),
}
```

It has `thinking` and `redacted_thinking` for the OpenAI Responses API reasoning content, but **no `reasoning` field for the legacy OpenAI Chat Completions `{"completion", "reasoning"}` shape**.

Then `ChatMlMessageSchema` is `BaseChatMlMessageSchema.refine(...).transform(({ additional_kwargs, ...other }) => ({ ...other, ...additional_kwargs })).transform(({ role, name, content, audio, type, tools, tool_calls, tool_call_id, thinking, redacted_thinking, ...other }) => ({ role, name, content, audio, type, tools

body:
### Summary
 
`web/src/features/comments/ReactionPicker.tsx` imports `@ferrucc-io/emoji-picker`, which until recently ran a synchronous canvas-based emoji support detection at module evaluation time. **On Windows with Chrome or Edge this blocks the main thread for roughly 5 seconds on page load** — even though the picker itself sits behind a `Popover` and is never rendered until the user clicks the trigger.
 
I tracked this down, submitted a fix upstream, and it has been merged and released:
 
- ferrucc-io/emoji-picker#114 (merged)
- Published as **0.1.2** on 2026-08-17

Langfuse pins `"@ferrucc-io/emoji-picker": "^0.0.47"` in `web/package.json`. Because `^0.0.x` is constrained to the `0.0.x` range under semver, this release will not be picked up automatically. **Bumping the pin to `^0.1.2` should be all that is needed.**
